title: Halving and Ordering
focus: Three ways to avoid looking at everything: discard half, keep only the best k, share the prefix.

cards.title: Binary Search
cards.trigger: A sorted array, or any monotonic predicate that flips from false to true exactly once.
cards.recall: Write the leftmost-boundary version from memory. Then say the loop invariant out loud: what is true about everything left of `lo` and everything right of `hi` at every iteration?
useWhen: Find a value, or the insertion point, in sorted data
First or last index satisfying a condition
Search a rotated or 2D sorted array
Peak finding on a bitonic sequence
Anything where you can test 'is k feasible' in O(n)
template: # Leftmost index where pred(i) is True. Memorise THIS one.
lo, hi = 0, len(nums)             # note: hi = n, half-open
else: hi = mid              # mid stays a candidate
return lo                        # in [0, n], may be n
keyInsights: Learn one boundary template cold. Exact match is a special case of it, never the reverse
`lo < hi` with `hi = mid` terminates. `lo <= hi` with `hi = mid` loops forever. That is the classic infinite loop
The answer of `lower_bound` can be n, meaning 'not present, insert at the end'. Check the bound before indexing
cards.trap: 'Now find the last index that is less than target.' If you memorised only the exact-match form you will fumble this. The boundary form is a one-character change.

cards.title: Heap / Priority Queue
patterns: Top k with a size-k heap
cards.trigger: You need the smallest or largest repeatedly, but you do not need the whole thing sorted.
cards.recall: Write the k-closest-points solution from memory. Then answer: to keep the k *smallest*, do you use a min-heap or a max-heap, and why is the intuitive answer wrong?
useWhen: Top k or kth largest, streaming or static
Merge k sorted sequences
Dijkstra and any greedy that always takes the current best
Scheduling by deadline, cost or frequency
Running median with two heaps
template: # k smallest: keep a MAX-heap of size k, evict the worst
heapq.heappush(h, -x)     # negate: Python only has min-heaps
heapq.heappop(h)      # drops the largest so far
# Tuples break ties left to right; add a counter if items are not comparable

complexity.time: O(n log k) for top k

keyInsights: To keep the k smallest you need a max-heap, because you must be able to evict the current worst. This inverts every time
Python has no max-heap. Negate the key, and remember to un-negate on the way out
`heapify` is O(n) but pushing n items one at a time is O(n log n). Build in bulk when you can
cards.trap: 'Do it in O(n) average.' That is Quickselect, not a heap. Know when they are fishing for the partition-based answer.

cards.title: Trie (Prefix Tree)
cards.trigger: Many strings, and the query is about prefixes rather than whole-string equality.
cards.recall: Write insert and search from memory. Then answer why `is_word` has to exist at all, given that the node already exists after inserting 'apple'.
useWhen: Autocomplete and prefix counting
Word search on a board with a large dictionary
Longest common prefix across many strings
Replace words with their shortest root
Bitwise problems, a binary trie over 32 bits for max XOR
template: if ch not in node.kids: return None
def search(self, w):        return (n := self._walk(w)) is not None and n.is_word
def starts_with(self, p):   return self._walk(p) is not None

complexity.time: O(L) per op, L = word length

keyInsights: `is_word` distinguishes 'app' inserted from 'app' merely being a prefix of 'apple'. Without it search is wrong
Lookup is O(L) independent of how many words are stored. That is the entire selling point over a hash set
For board search, walk the trie and the grid together so a dead prefix prunes the whole subtree at once
cards.trap: 'Support a `.` wildcard matching any character.' Search becomes DFS over all children at that position. Say the branching cost, O(26^dots).

cards.title: Take or Skip DP
cards.trigger: A sequence of choices where taking one item forbids a neighbouring item.
cards.recall: State what `dp[i]` means, then write the two-variable form. Then answer: for the circular version, why does running the linear solver twice work, and what are the two ranges?
useWhen: Non-adjacent maximum sum
Scheduling where adjacent slots conflict
Delete-and-earn style problems after a frequency transform
Any binary decision per index with a local constraint
Tree version, rob or skip each node
template: # dp[i] = best total considering the first i houses
take, skip = 0, 0        # take = best if we rob house i, skip = best if we do not
take, skip = skip + x, max(skip, take)
# Circular: house 0 and house n-1 are adjacent, so one of them is out
# Tree version: return a PAIR from every node
keyInsights: Two states per index, not one. Carrying 'best if I took it' separately is what makes the constraint expressible
The circular trick works because at least one of the two endpoints must be excluded, so the two runs cover every case
The tree version returns a tuple. Any time a constraint couples a node to its parent, return a pair
cards.trap: 'Delete and earn: taking value v deletes all v-1 and v+1.' Count frequencies into an array indexed by value, then this is literally house robber. Spotting the transform is the test.

cards.title: Union Find (DSU)
cards.trigger: Connectivity questions with no path needed, especially when edges arrive over time.
cards.recall: Write find and union with both optimisations from memory. Then answer: what is the actual complexity with both, and what does it degrade to with neither?
useWhen: Count connected components as edges are added
Detect a cycle in an undirected graph
Kruskal's minimum spanning tree
Account or email merging, equations for equality
Anything phrased as 'are these two in the same group'
template: if ra == rb: return False         # already joined -> a cycle
if self.r[ra] < self.r[rb]: ra, rb = rb, ra
keyInsights: `union` returning False is your cycle detector, and Kruskal's edge filter, for free
Track `count` inside the structure so component counting is O(1) instead of a final sweep
With only one optimisation you are at O(log n). With neither you are at O(n) and it is a linked list
cards.trap: 'Now support undo.' Path compression makes rollback impossible. You need union by rank only, plus a change log. Knowing why compression is the blocker is the answer.
